analysis.one_liner: Gives consumers rights to see, correct, and delete the personal data companies collect, enforced by the FTC.
analysis.headline: The bill got no cosponsors and never received a hearing, markup, or vote; it died in the Senate Commerce Committee when the 116th Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would require companies to get permission before collecting people's personal data, publish clear privacy policies, protect the data they hold, and let people see, correct, and delete their information. The Federal Trade Commission would enforce the rules, with civil penalties of up to $42,530 per affected person, and state attorneys general could also sue. The bill would wipe out state privacy laws in this area and block individuals from suing companies directly, leaving enforcement to the FTC and state AGs.
analysis.who_benefits: Ordinary consumers gain enforceable rights over their data: companies must get consent before collecting it, tell people what they hold, let them access, correct, and delete it, and delete or de-identify sensitive data when no longer needed. The FTC would get at least 440 new staff to enforce the rules. Businesses that comply cleanly get a single national rulebook instead of fifty different state laws.

how_it_helps.text: Companies may not collect or process personal data without consent, except for limited purposes like completing a transaction, complying with law, preventing fraud, or internal operations [S3].
Individuals can access a copy of their data, correct errors, and request deletion, free of charge at least twice a year [S3].

Companies holding large amounts of data must designate a privacy officer, run privacy impact assessments, and maintain a comprehensive security program; violations carry FTC civil penalties up to $42,530 per affected individual, and state attorneys general can also enforce [S3].
The FTC would appoint no fewer than 440 additional personnel to enforce privacy and data security laws [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Any company that collects or processes personal data bears new compliance costs: building security programs, publishing detailed privacy policies, honoring access and deletion requests, and exposure to civil penalties. The advertising and data-brokerage business model, which depends on aggregating people's information, would face the sharpest constraints. Small businesses under a defined size threshold get partial exemptions.
analysis.who_pays_short: Companies and advertisers trading in personal data

drawbacks.text: The bill explicitly creates no private right of action, so individuals could not sue companies that misuse their data; only the FTC and state attorneys general could enforce [S3].

It preempts and 'occupies the field' of state privacy law, overriding stronger state rules such as California's consumer privacy law, and it strips the Federal Communications Commission of authority over how broadband and telecom companies handle personal data [S3].

For ordinary (non-sensitive) data, mere failure to opt out counts as consent, so much data collection could continue by default; small businesses are exempt from the access and correction rights entirely [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill delivers real, enforceable rights that consumers have no federal equivalent for today, backed by meaningful per-person penalties. But its design tilts toward the companies it regulates: no individual lawsuits, a broad federal preemption that would cap stronger state laws, and an implicit-consent default for most data. An honest supporter would call it a genuine floor with a ceiling problem; critics on both the consumer and business sides found something to object to.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced in March 2020 and referred to the Senate Commerce Committee, which never held a hearing or vote, and the bill expired when the 116th Congress ended in January 2021.

narrative.text: Sen. Jerry Moran introduced the bill on March 12, 2020, and it was read twice and referred to the Committee on Commerce, Science, and Transportation [S5].
No senator signed on as a cosponsor [S4].
The committee took no further action; the bill's only recorded action after referral is the referral itself, and it never reached the Senate floor before the Congress ended [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Companies that collect and trade in consumer data avoided new federal duties, though they also lost the national preemption this bill offered; consumers are left with whatever state laws they happen to live under and no federal privacy rights.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Data brokers and platforms kept the status quo

for.name: Jerry Moran
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and saw it referred to the Commerce Committee; it was his bill alone, with no cosponsors.

against.name: Roger Wicker
against.role: Chair, Senate Committee on Commerce, Science, and Transportation
against.what_they_did: Never scheduled the bill for a hearing, markup, or committee vote, leaving it to die at the end of the Congress.

sides.party_line_note: No vote was ever taken and the bill had no cosponsors, so the partisan shape of support or opposition was never tested on the record.

industries.industry: Tech platforms, advertisers, and data brokers
industries.note: The bill would restrict how these companies collect and monetize personal data and expose them to FTC penalties. But it would also hand them a single national standard that preempts stricter state laws like California's, and it eliminates the threat of individual lawsuits, so parts of the bill entrench their position.

Businesses under 500 employees with under $50 million in receipts are exempt from the access and correction rights and get extra leeway on deletion and enforcement, sparing them compliance costs their larger competitors would bear.

The bill removes FCC authority over how these companies handle personal data, leaving them subject only to this law's FTC-enforced rules — a lighter touch than the communications regulator had applied.
